## Overview {#sec-topic3-overview}

<!-- Chapter content goes here -->

## Compartmental models

Simple models for the spread of infectious diseases are often based on the idea of **compartments**. Individuals in a population are classified into different compartments based on their disease status, and the model describes how individuals move between compartments over time.

Common compartments include: Susceptible (available for infection, $S$), Infected (and Infectious!, $I$), and Recovered (or Removed, $R$). The dynamics of the disease can be described using differential equations that govern the rates of change between these compartments.

In most cases, one considers the total population fixed (the dynamics of the disease are rapid compared to the dynamics of the population), so that $S + I + R = N$ is constant, and $N=1$ without loss of generality (i.e., compartments represent the proportion of the population in each state). The simplest model is the **SIR model**, which assumes that individuals move from being susceptible to infected, and then to recovered. This model was proposed by Kermack and McKendrick in 1927, and is still widely used today, despite being exactly a century old! 

Many variations on this basic framework exist, including models that account for births and deaths, vaccination, waning immunity, and more. The SIR model is a foundational tool in epidemiology and provides insights into the dynamics of infectious diseases.

## Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model

The population is divided into three compartments: Susceptible ($S$), Infected ($I$), and Recovered ($R$). Susceptible individuals can become infected upon contact with infected individuals, and infected individuals can recover from the disease, thereby gaining long-lasting immunity. The model is best understood using boxes and arrows to represent the flow of individuals between compartments:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sir-diagram
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "Flow diagram of the SIR model. Susceptible individuals ($S$) become infected at rate $\\beta S I$ upon contact with infectious individuals ($I$), who recover at rate $\\gamma I$."
plot_sir_diagram()
```

The dynamics of the SIR model can be described by the following set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta S I\\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta S I - \gamma I\\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I
\end{aligned}
$$

The dynamics of this model are governed by two key parameters: the transmission rate $\beta$ and the recovery rate $\gamma$. $\beta$ can be thought of as the rate at which susceptible individuals become infected upon contact with infectious individuals, while $\gamma$ is the rate at which infected individuals recover and move to the recovered compartment (for example, the reciprocal of the average infectious period). The trajectories of the compartments cannot be solved analytically in general, but can be simulated numerically. However, we can make sense of the dynamics by considering that a) the number of susceptible individuals can only decrease over time, and b) the number of infected individuals can increase or decrease depending on the relative sizes of the susceptible and infected compartments. In particular:

$$
\frac{1}{I} \frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S - \gamma
$$

and thus the number of infected individuals will increase when $\beta S/\gamma > 1$. Suppose that the population is initially entirely susceptible, so that $S \approx 1$. Then the condition for the number of infected individuals to increase is $\beta/\gamma > 1$, which leads to the concept of the **basic reproduction number** $\mathcal{R}_0 = \beta / \gamma$, which determines whether an infection will spread in a population. If $\mathcal{R}_0 > 1$, the infection can invade and cause an epidemic; if $\mathcal{R}_0 < 1$, the infection will die out. This quantity can be interpreted as the average number of secondary infections produced by a single infected individual in a completely susceptible population. The basic reproduction number is a fundamental concept in epidemiology and is used to assess the potential for disease outbreaks and to inform public health interventions.

With these qualitiative insights, we can now explore the dynamics of the SIR model in more detail, including the effects of varying parameters and initial conditions on the spread of infectious diseases. 

### Dynamics of the SIR model {#sec-topic3-sir-dynamics}

The figure below shows the dynamics of the model for $\beta = 2$ and $\gamma = 1$, so that $\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$. The left panel shows the proportion of the population in each compartment through time, starting from a small number of infected individuals ($I_0 = 0.01$). The right panel shows the same trajectory in the **phase plane**, with the susceptible proportion on the horizontal axis and the infected proportion on the vertical axis: time is not shown explicitly, but the trajectory is traced from the filled dot, and the grey arrows show the direction in which the system moves from any given state. The orange dashed line marks $S = \gamma/\beta$, the value of $S$ at which $dI/dt = 0$.

In the interactive version, move the slider to change the initial fraction of susceptible individuals $S_0$; the remaining individuals ($1 - S_0 - I_0$) start in the recovered class, and are therefore immune. Try starting with a fully susceptible population ($S_0$ close to 1), and then progressively reduce $S_0$. In the PDF version, three representative values of $S_0$ are shown. As you do so, pay attention to three things: whether an epidemic occurs at all, how high the peak of $I$ is, and how many susceptible individuals remain at the end.

```{r}
#| label: sir-dynamics-grid
#| include: false
sir_grid <- .sir_dynamics_grid()
ojs_define(sir_traj = sir_grid$traj, sir_vfield = sir_grid$vfield)
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{ojs}
viewof sir_i = Inputs.range([1, 99], {step: 1, value: 99,
  label: "Initial susceptible S₀"})

{
  const S0    = sir_i / 100;
  const Rinit = (1 - S0 - 0.01).toFixed(2);
  const rows  = transpose(sir_traj).filter(d => d.i === sir_i);
  const vf    = transpose(sir_vfield);

  const tlong = rows.flatMap(d => [
    {t: d.t, comp: "S", val: d.S},
    {t: d.t, comp: "I", val: d.I},
    {t: d.t, comp: "R", val: d.R}
  ]);

  const pal = {domain: ["S","I","R"], range: ["#2980b9","#e74c3c","#27ae60"]};

  const lp = Plot.plot({
    width: 360, height: 290,
    x: {label: "Time (t)"},
    y: {label: "Proportion", domain: [0, 1]},
    color: {...pal, legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(tlong, {x: "t", y: "val", stroke: "comp", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });

  const rp = Plot.plot({
    width: 360, height: 290,
    x: {label: "Susceptible (S)", domain: [0, 1]},
    y: {label: "Infected (I)",    domain: [0, 0.3]},
    marks: [
      Plot.arrow(vf, {x1:"S", y1:"I", x2:"S2", y2:"I2",
        stroke:"#ccc", strokeWidth:0.8, headLength:4}),
      Plot.ruleX([0.5], {stroke:"#e67e22", strokeDasharray:"5,3", strokeWidth:1.2}),
      Plot.line(rows, {x:"S", y:"I", stroke:"#444", strokeWidth:2}),
      Plot.dot([{S: S0, I: 0.01}], {x:"S", y:"I", r:5, fill:"#444"})
    ]
  });

  return html`<div>
    <p style="font-size:0.87em;margin:0 0 5px">
      <strong>S₀ = ${S0.toFixed(2)}</strong>, I₀ = 0.01,
      initial recovered = ${Rinit};&ensp;β = 2, γ = 1
    </p>
    <div style="display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:flex-start">${lp}${rp}</div>
    <p style="font-size:0.82em;color:#666;margin:4px 0 0">
      Orange dashed line: herd immunity threshold S = γ/β = 0.5.
      Filled dot marks the initial state; trajectory moves leftward as S decreases.
    </p>
  </div>`;
}
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-sir-dynamics-static
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "SIR model dynamics for three initial susceptible fractions ($S_0 = 0.25, 0.65, 0.95$), with $I_0 = 0.01$, $\\beta = 2$, $\\gamma = 1$ ($\\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$). When $S_0 < \\gamma/\\beta = 0.5$ the infection dies out immediately; when $S_0 > 0.5$ an epidemic develops. Interactive version: https://your-course-site#sec-topic3-sir-dynamics."
plot_sir_dynamics_static()
```
:::

What do we learn from the figure?

First, **an epidemic occurs only if $S_0 > \gamma/\beta$**. To the right of the dashed line in the phase plane, $dI/dt > 0$ and the arrows point upward; to the left, $dI/dt < 0$ and the arrows point downward. A trajectory starting to the left of the line (with $S_0 < \gamma/\beta = 1/\mathcal{R}_0$) can only move further left, and the infection declines from the outset. This is the idea behind **herd immunity**: if a sufficiently large fraction of the population is immune at the start, an introduced infection cannot spread, even though most individuals could in principle be infected.

Second, **the epidemic peaks exactly when $S$ crosses $\gamma/\beta$**. When $S_0 > \gamma/\beta$, the infection initially grows exponentially, because each infected individual replaces itself with more than one new infection. As the epidemic proceeds, susceptible individuals are depleted, and $S$ decreases until it reaches $\gamma/\beta$: at this point each infected individual only replaces itself, and $I$ reaches its maximum. Note that the epidemic starts to decline while most of the population is still susceptible (for $S_0 \approx 1$ and $\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$, half of the population is susceptible at the peak, and the proportion of infected individuals is about 16%). The epidemic subsides not because everyone has been infected, but because infected individuals are now too rarely in contact with susceptible ones to sustain transmission.

Third, **the epidemic overshoots**. After the peak, $I$ declines but is still positive, so that new infections continue to occur and $S$ keeps decreasing, ending well below $\gamma/\beta$. In the phase plane, the trajectory continues to the left of the dashed line until $I$ vanishes on the horizontal axis. We have thus a counterintuitive result: lowering the susceptible proportion just below the threshold would be enough to stop the epidemic, but the epidemic itself reduces it far more. How far is determined by $\mathcal{R}_0$, as we will see in the next section.

Finally, note the effect of the initial condition: reducing $S_0$ by moving individuals to the recovered class (as would be done by vaccination) lowers the peak, makes the epidemic smaller, and delays it, until, for $S_0 < \gamma/\beta$, it disappears entirely. We will return to this point in the section on vaccination.

## Number of people experiencing infection over time

The SIR model cannot be solved analytically, but we can determine what fraction of the population was infected over the entire course of an epidemic — the **final attack rate** — without integrating the differential equations. As $t \to \infty$ the epidemic subsides: $I(\infty) = 0$, so all individuals are either susceptible or recovered, and $S(\infty) + R(\infty) = 1$.

To find $S(\infty)$, we eliminate time from the ODEs by computing

$$
\frac{dS}{dR} = \frac{dS/dt}{dR/dt} = \frac{-\beta S I}{\gamma I} = -\frac{\beta}{\gamma} S = -\mathcal{R}_0 \, S.
$$

This separable equation integrates to $S(t) = S_0 \exp(-\mathcal{R}_0 (R(t) - R(0)))$. Starting from a nearly fully susceptible population ($S_0 \approx 1$, $R(0) = 0$), and taking $t \to \infty$ with $R(\infty) = 1 - S(\infty)$, we obtain the **final size relation**:

$$
S(\infty) = \exp\!\bigl(-\mathcal{R}_0 \,(1 - S(\infty))\bigr).
$$ {#eq-sir-final-size}

This is a fixed-point equation: the right-hand side depends on $S(\infty)$ itself, so it cannot be solved algebraically. It can, however, be solved numerically for any given $\mathcal{R}_0$. The final attack rate $1 - S(\infty)$ is plotted as a function of $\mathcal{R}_0$ in @fig-sir-final-size.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sir-final-size
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Final attack rate $1 - S(\\infty)$ as a function of $\\mathcal{R}_0$, obtained by solving @eq-sir-final-size numerically. Below the epidemic threshold $\\mathcal{R}_0 = 1$ (red dashed line) the infection always dies out; above it a non-zero fraction of the population is infected. For $\\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$, approximately 80% of a fully susceptible population is eventually infected before the epidemic ends. Dashed curves: approximation close to the threshold (@eq-final-size-small) and for large $\\mathcal{R}_0$ (@eq-final-size-large)."
plot_sir_final_size()
```

A striking feature of @eq-sir-final-size is that the final attack rate is entirely determined by $\mathcal{R}_0$, regardless of the individual values of $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Two diseases with different transmission and recovery rates but the same $\mathcal{R}_0$ will infect the same total fraction of the population — even though their time courses may look very different.

To see how $\mathcal{R}_0$ influences the final attack rate, it helps to solve @eq-sir-final-size approximately in two limits. Let $z = 1 - S(\infty)$ be the final attack rate, so that $1 - z = e^{-\mathcal{R}_0 z}$.

**Large $\mathcal{R}_0$.** When $\mathcal{R}_0$ is large nearly everybody is infected, so $z \approx 1$ and $\log S(\infty) = -\mathcal{R}_0 z \approx -\mathcal{R}_0$. The fraction of the population that escapes infection is

$$
S(\infty) \approx e^{-\mathcal{R}_0},
$$ {#eq-final-size-large}

which decays exponentially with $\mathcal{R}_0$: for $\mathcal{R}_0 = 3$ roughly 5% of the population escapes the epidemic, and for $\mathcal{R}_0 = 5$ less than 1% does. This is the regime of measles, for which essentially everybody not immunized is infected.

**Close to the threshold.** When $\mathcal{R}_0 = 1 + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon$ small, the attack rate $z$ is also small, and we can expand the exponential to second order, $1 - z \approx 1 - \mathcal{R}_0 z + \mathcal{R}_0^2 z^2/2$. Dividing by $z$ and rearranging gives

$$
z \approx \frac{2(\mathcal{R}_0 - 1)}{\mathcal{R}_0^2} \approx 2 (\mathcal{R}_0 - 1),
$$ {#eq-final-size-small}

so just above the threshold the attack rate grows linearly with $\mathcal{R}_0 - 1$, with slope 2: a pathogen with $\mathcal{R}_0 = 1.1$ infects about 17% of the population (@eq-final-size-small gives 17%, the rougher $2(\mathcal{R}_0-1)$ gives 20%).

In short: for $\mathcal{R}_0 \gtrsim 3$ use @eq-final-size-large, and for $\mathcal{R}_0 \lesssim 1.3$ use @eq-final-size-small. In between, solve @eq-sir-final-size numerically. @fig-sir-final-size compares the two approximations with the exact solution.

## Vaccination

Vaccination is the most effective tool we have against infectious diseases, and the SIR model makes it easy to understand why. Suppose that, before the pathogen arrives, a fraction $p$ of the population is vaccinated with a vaccine that confers complete and lasting protection. Vaccinated individuals can neither be infected nor transmit, so they behave exactly like individuals who have recovered: they start in the $R$ compartment. The initial condition is then $S_0 = 1 - p$ (we neglect the small initial fraction of infected individuals), which is precisely what we changed with the slider in the figure of the previous section. Vaccination does not change the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ of the model, only the initial proportion of susceptible individuals.

Recall that the number of infected individuals grows when $\beta S/\gamma > 1$. We call the quantity

$$
\mathcal{R}_{\text{eff}} = \mathcal{R}_0 \, S
$$ {#eq-reff}

the **effective reproduction number**: the average number of secondary infections caused by an infected individual when a fraction $S$ of the population is susceptible. In a vaccinated population, a single infected individual introduced in the population has $\mathcal{R}_{\text{eff}} = \mathcal{R}_0 (1 - p)$. The infection can invade only if this exceeds 1, and thus the epidemic is prevented when $\mathcal{R}_0(1 - p) < 1$, i.e., when the vaccination coverage exceeds the **critical vaccination threshold**

$$
p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{\mathcal{R}_0}.
$$ {#eq-critical-vaccination}

This is the same condition, $S_0 < \gamma/\beta$, that we found when exploring the dynamics of the model. The threshold depends on the pathogen only through $\mathcal{R}_0$, and increases quickly with it: for $\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$ it is enough to immunize half of the population, but for $\mathcal{R}_0 = 15$ more than 93% of individuals must be immune (@tbl-critical-coverage).

| Disease | $\mathcal{R}_0$ (approximate) | Critical threshold $p_c$ |
|---|---|---|
| Smallpox | 3–6 | 67–83% |
| Polio | 5–7 | 80–86% |
| Measles | 12–18 | 92–94% |

: Approximate critical vaccination thresholds from @eq-critical-vaccination. The values of $\mathcal{R}_0$ are rough estimates, and vary among populations. {#tbl-critical-coverage}

This is the phenomenon of **herd immunity**: when more than a fraction $p_c$ of the population is immune, the infection cannot spread, and the individuals who cannot be vaccinated (e.g., newborns, immunocompromised individuals) are protected indirectly, because most of the people they come in contact with cannot transmit the disease. Herd immunity is a property of the population, not of individuals: the unvaccinated are safe only as long as the vaccinated majority is large enough, and only if they are surrounded by it.

Coverage below $p_c$ does not prevent the epidemic, but it is still useful, because it makes the epidemic smaller. Since vaccinated individuals start in the recovered class, the final size relation generalizes to

$$
S(\infty) = S_0 \exp\!\bigl(-\mathcal{R}_0 \,(S_0 - S(\infty))\bigr), \qquad S_0 = 1 - p,
$$

as can be seen by repeating the derivation of the previous section without assuming $S_0 \approx 1$. @fig-vaccination-final-size shows the fraction of the population that is eventually infected as a function of coverage. For $\mathcal{R}_0 = 2$, immunizing a quarter of the population reduces the fraction ever infected from about 80% to 44%; at $p = p_c$ the epidemic disappears. For a pathogen with a large $\mathcal{R}_0$, however, the curve falls slowly at first: for $\mathcal{R}_0 = 15$, vaccinating half of the population still leaves 50% of it infected, and the threshold is reached only at 93% coverage.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vaccination-final-size
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of the population eventually infected, $S_0 - S(\\infty)$, as a function of the fraction immunized before the epidemic, for three values of $\\mathcal{R}_0$. Dashed vertical lines mark the critical vaccination threshold $p_c = 1 - 1/\\mathcal{R}_0$ (@eq-critical-vaccination), above which no epidemic occurs."
plot_vaccination_final_size()
```

Two complications make eradication harder than @eq-critical-vaccination suggests. First, vaccines are not perfect: if a vaccine protects a fraction $e$ of the individuals who receive it (its *efficacy*), the fraction immune is $e p$, and the threshold on coverage becomes $p_c = (1 - 1/\mathcal{R}_0)/e$. For $\mathcal{R}_0 = 15$ and $e = 0.95$, one needs to vaccinate more than 98% of the population; if $e < 1 - 1/\mathcal{R}_0$, no level of coverage can stop transmission, which is why measles vaccination requires a second dose. Second, the model assumes that individuals mix uniformly, so that only the average coverage matters. In reality, unvaccinated individuals are often clustered in space or in social groups: a country can have a national coverage above $p_c$ and still have communities well below it, in which outbreaks can occur. The examples below illustrate how these ideas play out for three diseases.


::: {.callout-note}
## The eradication of smallpox

Smallpox is the only human disease that has been eradicated. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the World Health Assembly declared the world free of smallpox. The figure below shows the number of cases reported to the World Health Organization each year.

```{r}
#| label: fig-smallpox
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Smallpox cases reported worldwide, 1920–1980. Data: WHO, compiled by Our World in Data. Dashed lines mark the start of the intensified eradication programme (1967) and the last natural case (1977). Reported cases are a small fraction of the true number: WHO estimated about 15 million cases in 1967, against roughly 130,000 reported."
plot_smallpox_cases()
```

Why was smallpox such a good target? Humans are the only host of the virus, so there is no animal reservoir from which it can re-invade. Infections are not silent: infected individuals develop a recognizable rash and are infectious mostly after it appears, so cases can be found, isolated, and the contacts of each case vaccinated ("ring vaccination") instead of vaccinating everybody. Survivors are immune for life, and the vaccine is cheap and stable. Finally, the basic reproduction number is moderate (typically estimated between 3 and 6), so that the fraction that must be immune to prevent spread, $1 - 1/\mathcal{R}_0$, is relatively low.
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## The resurgence of measles in the United States

Measles is one of the most transmissible human pathogens, with $\mathcal{R}_0$ typically estimated between 12 and 18, so that vaccination coverage of roughly 95% is needed to prevent outbreaks. The figure below shows the number of reported cases in the United States since 1938.

```{r}
#| label: fig-us-measles
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Reported measles cases in the US, 1938–2026 (log scale). Data from the CDC and earlier public health reports, compiled by Our World in Data. Dashed lines mark the licensure of the first measles vaccine (1963) and the declaration that measles was eliminated from the US (2000). The 2026 count (open circle) is incomplete: it covers cases through October 1."
plot_us_measles()
```

Before the vaccine, hundreds of thousands of cases were reported every year. The introduction of the vaccine in 1963 led to a dramatic decline in measles cases.

Note the spike in the number of cases in the period 1989–1991. The cause of this spike was attributed to low vaccination coverage among low-income, inner-city preschool-aged children who had not received their single recommended dose due to healthcare access barriers, underfunded public health infrastructure, and missed vaccination opportunities. In 1989, the CDC recommended adding a second dose of MMR before school entry. This was introduced because ~2–5% of individuals failed to develop immunity after a single dose (primary vaccine failure). This allowed to reach the minimum number of cases in recorded history, and in 2000 endemic transmission had stopped.

Vaccination coverage among kindergartners has been reported by the CDC since the 2009–10 school year (@fig-us-kindergarten-mmr). National coverage with MMR hovered around the 95% needed to block transmission until 2019–20, and has since fallen steadily, while the fraction of children with an exemption from one or more vaccines has risen to its highest level on record.

Since then, imported cases have found pockets of unvaccinated individuals, and the numbers have risen again: 2025 saw 2,289 cases, and by October 2026 the count was the highest since 1991. Why does a small decline in vaccination coverage, which may look harmless, have such a large effect on a disease with a very high $\mathcal{R}_0$?

```{r}
#| label: fig-us-kindergarten-mmr
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "MMR vaccination coverage (left) and exemption rate (right) among US kindergartners, school years 2009–10 to 2025–26. The dashed line marks 95% coverage. Data: CDC SchoolVaxView (state-reported); the 2010–11 school year was not reported. Note that coverage is measured at school entry."
plot_us_kindergarten_mmr()
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Why is the eradication of polio within reach?

Polio is the second disease, after smallpox, that humanity is close to eradicating. When the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate it in 1988, polio paralyzed hundreds of thousands of children each year in more than 125 countries. Today wild poliovirus type 1 is endemic only in Afghanistan and Pakistan, and the other two wild types have been declared eradicated (type 2 in 2015, type 3 in 2019).

```{r}
#| label: fig-wild-polio
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Paralytic polio cases reported worldwide, 1980–2024 (log scale). Data: WHO via Our World in Data for 1980–2023 (cases from wild poliovirus only from 2001), and GPEI for 2024. The dashed line marks the 1988 resolution to eradicate polio. Reported cases are only a fraction of the true number: in 1988 about 350,000 cases were estimated."
plot_wild_polio_cases()
```

The reasons for optimism are the same that made smallpox a good target. Poliovirus infects only humans and does not persist for long in the environment, so there is no reservoir. Immunity after infection or vaccination is long-lasting, and effective, inexpensive vaccines exist. The basic reproduction number is moderate (typically estimated between 5 and 7), so that coverage of roughly 80–85% is enough to stop transmission, compared with more than 90% for measles.

Polio is harder than smallpox in one respect: fewer than 1 in 100 infections causes paralysis, so for each reported case hundreds of infections go unnoticed. This is why surveillance of paralysis must be complemented by testing of wastewater, and why a single case signals widespread transmission. Another difficulty is that the oral vaccine contains a weakened virus that, in under-immunized populations, can circulate for long enough to regain its ability to cause paralysis. These vaccine-derived cases are why the number of paralytic cases was not zero in recent years even though wild poliovirus has retreated to two countries.
:::




## Other compartmental models

A common variation on the SIR model is the inclusiong of demography. Newborns enter the population as susceptible individuals, and all individuals experience a natural death rate. This leads to the **SIR model with demography**, which can be described by the following set of ODEs:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sir-demography-diagram
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "SIR model with demography. Newborns enter the susceptible class at constant rate $\\Lambda$; all compartments experience natural mortality at per-capita rate $\\mu$."
plot_sir_demography_diagram()
```


$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= \Lambda - \beta S I - \mu S\\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta S I - \gamma I - \mu I\\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I - \mu R
\end{aligned}
$$

In this model if $\Lambda = \mu$, the total population size remains constant, and the dynamics of the disease are similar to those of the basic SIR model. However, if $\Lambda > \mu$, the population grows over time, while if $\Lambda < \mu$, the population declines.

A simpler version of the model is the **SIS model**, which assumes that individuals do not gain long-lasting immunity after infection. In this case, individuals move from the Susceptible compartment to the Infected compartment and back again, without ever entering the Recovered compartment. The dynamics of the SIS model can be described by the following set of ODEs:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sis-diagram
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "Flow diagram of the SIS model. Recovered individuals return immediately to the susceptible class at rate $\\gamma I$, conferring no lasting immunity."
plot_sis_diagram()
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta S I + \gamma I\\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta S I - \gamma I
\end{aligned}
$$

For diseases that do not confer long-lasting immunity, individuals may move from the Recovered compartment back to the Susceptible compartment. This leads to the **SIRS model**, which includes a waning immunity term. Other models may include additional compartments, such as Exposed (E) for diseases with a latent period, leading to the SEIR model, leading to the follwing set of ODEs:

```{r}
#| label: fig-seir-diagram
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "SEIR model with waning immunity. Exposed individuals ($E$) progress to infectious at rate $\\sigma E$; recovered individuals ($R$) lose immunity and re-enter the susceptible class at rate $\\delta R$."
plot_seir_diagram()
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta S I + \delta R\\
\frac{dE}{dt} &= \beta S I - \sigma E\\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \sigma E - \gamma I\\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I - \delta R
\end{aligned}
$$


You can find more complex models in which some compartments represent a disease vector (e.g., mosquitoes) or a pathogen (e.g., free-living bacteria) in the environment. These models are often referred to as **vector-borne** or **environmental transmission** models, respectively. While the number of compartments and the complexity of the models can vary widely, the basic principles of compartmental modeling remain the same: individuals move between compartments based on rates that depend on the current state of the system. 

@fig-zika-model shows a more complex example from @roosa2019identifiability: a model of **Zika virus transmission** that couples two interacting populations — humans and mosquitoes. The human population is divided into susceptible ($S_h$), exposed ($E_h$), asymptomatically infectious ($A_h$), symptomatically infectious ($I_{h1}$), convalescent ($I_{h2}$), and recovered ($R_h$) classes. Mosquitoes are divided into susceptible ($S_v$), exposed ($E_v$), and infectious ($I_v$) classes. Transmission is bidirectional: infectious mosquitoes ($I_v$) infect susceptible humans ($S_h$), and infectious humans ($A_h$, $I_{h1}$) infect susceptible mosquitoes ($S_v$).
